metadata.title: Why the Car That Crumples Saves You
metadata.register: formal, undergrad/grad audience, no casual narration
metadata.branding: none — unbranded, book content only, no channel/logo/handle

beats.narration_text: Two cars hit a wall at the same speed. Why is the passenger in the car that crumples safer?
beats.new_visual_element: Portrait-only opening question card (title-styled, crimson underline).

beats.narration_text: Two identical cars head toward a wall at the same speed. One has a rigid front end. The other has a front end designed to crumple. Which one would you rather be riding in?
beats.new_visual_element: Two side-view cars in stacked lanes facing a thick wall on the right: a vermilion car labeled RIGID and a teal car with an accordion-folded front labeled CRUMPLE ZONE, each with a passenger in the window and an equal velocity arrow v.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: two lanes, two cars with passengers, wall, equal velocity arrows

beats.narration_text: The rigid car stops almost instantly. Its passenger's momentum drops to zero in a tiny interval of time, so the average force needed to stop the passenger is enormous.
beats.new_visual_element: The rigid car drives into the wall and stops dead in one frame. A long vermilion force arrow snaps out above the passenger, pointing backward, labeled large force; a clock with a thin shaded sliver is labeled short Δt.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: rigid car stopped at the wall with a long backward force arrow and short-Δt clock; crumple car still waiting

beats.narration_text: The crumpling car folds as it stops, so the stop takes longer. The passenger has the same mass and the same change in speed, but that change is now spread over a longer time, and the average force is much smaller.
beats.new_visual_element: The crumple car reaches the wall; its accordion front compresses in four discrete steps while the car slows to rest. A short teal force arrow grows over the same stretch, labeled small force; its clock is mostly shaded, labeled long Δt.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: both cars stopped: rigid with long force arrow and short Δt, crumple with compressed front, short force arrow and long Δt

beats.narration_text: On a graph of force against time, the area of each rectangle is the impulse, the average force times the time interval. By the impulse-momentum theorem, the impulse equals the change in momentum, which is the same for both passengers. A tall, narrow rectangle and a short, wide one enclose the same area.
beats.new_visual_element: Two force-versus-time graphs with identical scales: a tall narrow vermilion rectangle (rigid) and a short wide teal rectangle (crumple), each filling in from left to right. Beneath: J = F̄ Δt = Δp, the same for both.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: two F–t graphs with equal-area rectangles, impulse equation

beats.narration_text: That is why crumple zones are not a weakness. The change in momentum is fixed by the crash, so the only way to reduce the average force is to extend the stopping time.
beats.new_visual_element: Back to both cars stopped at the wall: a vermilion starburst marks the rigid car's passenger, a calm teal circle the crumple car's passenger. Text: crumple zone: more time, less force.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: final held frame: both cars at the wall, danger and safe markers, summary text
